title: Colab, notebooks and version control
text: read the Week 2 Lecturer Runsheet first. Confirm Room wifi before the session; with ~100 students on Colab in Room 106 that is the single biggest risk. If Colab is unreachable, fall back to the offline bundle and lab machines — the runsheet has the contingency tree. Have the four Break and Fix notebooks ready to share.

title: LEARNING OBJECTIVES
text: read them out. Come back to this slide in the last five minutes and ask for a show of hands on each. It converts a busy practical session into visible progress.

title: HOW TODAY RUNS
text: say the break time out loud. In a practical session students will not ask, and they will start drifting out if they do not know when it is.

title: SEGMENT 1
text: collect A1 at the door. Then two minutes of recall — do not re-teach it.

title: CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING
text: thirty seconds in pairs, then take answers from three different people rather than the first hand up.

title: How did you do?
text: if more than a third of the room struggles with the first one, spend three minutes re-showing the Week 1 data-table figure. Everything from Week 5 assumes it and it is cheaper to fix now.

title: SEGMENT 2
text: introduce every tool by its question, never by its name.

title: THE TOOL MAP
text: if asked about VS Code — it is the professional local editor and the Student Setup Guide covers it. Anyone who wants a local setup is welcome. Note that the Week 7 and Week 14 tests run offline on lab machines, so everyone meets a local environment at least once.

title: DEFINITION
text: say the limitation out loud now rather than letting them discover it in Week 7.

title: SEGMENT 3
text: lockstep, projected, everyone typing along. Do NOT hand out a finished notebook at this stage; the typing is where the structure is learned. Circulate constantly and watch for students who have not got Colab open at all.

title: LIVE CODING
text: type it yourself on the projector, do not paste. Narrate as you go. When someone's cell 3 gives a different number from their neighbour's, that is the moment the execution-order block pays off — note who noticed.

title: TROUBLESHOOTING
text: put this slide up and leave it up during the practical rather than reading it aloud. It answers most questions before they are asked, which frees you to help the students who have a real problem.

title: DEFINITION
text: two minutes. Have them add one text cell above each code cell in the notebook they just built, saying what it does.

title: CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING
text: this is a pulse check, not an assessment. Take it verbally and quickly — the point is to catch anyone who has been quietly lost for twenty minutes.

title: How did you do?
text: if someone in the room has already noticed this discrepancy in their own work, name them when you reach the execution-order block. It lands far better coming from a student.

title: SEGMENT 4
text: keep it to twenty minutes and get them back on keyboards.

title: The anatomy of a notebook
text: draw the kernel on the board as a box that all the cells write into. Drawn beats projected for this one.

title: DEFINITION
text: have them look at their own counters right now. Several will already be out of order from experimenting, which makes the point better than any explanation.

title: SEGMENT 5
text: this is the highest-value twenty minutes of the session. If you are running late, take the time from the repository walkthrough rather than from here.

title: THE EXECUTION TRAP
text: let the room discover it before you explain. Ask 'is the notebook broken?' and wait. Someone will get there.

title: CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING
text: ninety seconds in pairs, then take B properly.

title: How did you do?
text: say plainly that this is not a rule you invented to be difficult. It is how every automated grader and every colleague will run their code.

title: WORKED EXAMPLE
text: walk it slowly. Then ask a student to read out their own counters and diagnose their own notebook, which makes it real.

title: 10 minutes
text: take it. Ninety minutes in, attention is genuinely gone, and Git needs them awake.

title: SEGMENT 6
text: lead with the problem, not the commands. Students who do not understand what Git is FOR treat it as ceremony and never use it voluntarily.

title: VERSION CONTROL
text: that line usually gets a laugh because everyone has done it — use it, the problem is familiar even though the solution is not. Be explicit about the assessment consequence; students engage with Git far more readily once they understand it is how their individual contribution is seen.

title: THE FOUR STATES
text: 'git status' is the single most useful command in the list. Tell them to run it before and after everything for the first fortnight.

title: DEFINITION
text: show one good and one useless commit message side by side on the board. It takes thirty seconds and it changes their habits for the semester.

title: SEGMENT 7
text: lockstep on the projector, line by line, everyone at the same step. Individually this takes three times as long and half the room ends up lost. Do not let the fast students run ahead.

title: LIVE CODING
text: do the menu route with the whole room first so everyone has a URL. Then demonstrate the four commands once on the projector. Do not make them use the command line today — it doubles the failure surface for no gain.

title: WHAT YOU OWE ME
text: the exact repository name matters — the grading tools pull repositories by name from a roster. State it and put it on the board.

title: THE README
text: show one good and one empty README on the projector. Thirty seconds, and it visibly changes what gets submitted.

title: CHALLENGE
text: the four planted faults: (1) an import of a package that is not installed; (2) a notebook reading a file by a path that is only correct from a different folder; (3) a cell that uses a variable created in a cell further down, so it only works if you run them out of order; (4) cells saved after being run out of order, so it produces a confident wrong number with no error at all. Fault four is the one to spend the last three minutes on. Circulate and ask only the six questions. Do not diagnose for them. Build the notebooks before the session; the runsheet has the specification.

title: QUIZ AND ASSIGNMENT
text: read the setup question's responses first. Anyone answering 'I do not know what is wrong' or 'I could not get that far' is your office-hours list this week, and that list is the highest-return thirty minutes of the semester. Question bank: scripts/quiz_bank_weeks.py, Week 2.

title: SEGMENT 8
text: say that the deck continues past the end of the session. Students do not read past the last slide you present unless told to.

title: MODULE SUMMARY
text: return to the objectives slide after this and ask for a show of hands against each.

title: How did you do?
text: answer E is the one to read aloud. Students respect being told the reasoning behind a rule rather than just the rule.

text: open the Form, project the QR, and give it exactly five minutes. Afterwards look at the responses-by-question view — any question most of the room got wrong is next week's five-minute reteach.

title: THE ONE THING TO REMEMBER
text: say the body text out loud and mean it. For a room of beginners this is the most useful thing they hear all week. Then stay behind for ten minutes — the students who need the most help will not ask in front of everyone.

text: check A2 at the door — repository URL, notebook runs, README present. Anyone without a working setup goes on the office-hours list now, not in Week 5.

title: LEARNING OBJECTIVES
text: read them out, and return to this slide at the end.

title: SEGMENT 1
text: two minutes of recall, then move. Do not re-teach Week 2.

title: CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING
text: thirty seconds in pairs. If the first question is shaky, the Week 2 deck's cheat-sheet slide has it.

title: SEGMENT 2
text: take the question seriously. A calculator IS faster for one calculation, and pretending otherwise loses you the sceptics in the room — who are usually the best students.

title: TODAY STARTS WITH AN OBJECTION
text: ask the room for the answer before you give it. Someone usually says 'because you can do it lots of times', which is exactly right and better received from a student.

title: WHY BOTHER
text: labour reason three. Make the Week 10 connection explicitly; students engage far better with syntax when they can see what it is for.

title: SEGMENT 3
text: twenty-five minutes is enough. They learn this by writing it, not by hearing it.

title: VARIABLES
text: draw the box on the board and physically write a value into it, then rub it out and write another. Thirty seconds, and it lands better than any slide.

title: DEFINITION
text: demonstrate "12" + 3 live and let them read the error. It is the same TypeError they will see next week.

title: WHAT GOES WRONG
text: demonstrate 0.1 + 0.2 live. It reliably produces an audible reaction and it makes the point permanently.

title: SEGMENT 4
text: type it live, do not paste. Narrate the units as you go. The typing is where the structure is learned.

title: The parts of a function
text: ask 'what will this print?' after typing only the definition. Answer: nothing. Let that land before you add the call.

title: WORKED EXAMPLE
text: do steps 1 to 4 on the board, out loud, before opening Colab. It takes three minutes and it makes the live-coding segment much faster because the thinking is already done.

title: LIVE CODING
text: type it, run it, confirm the output matches. THEN make the deliberate mistake and let the wrong number sit on screen for a few seconds before anyone speaks. Ask: what would have told you this was wrong? Physical intuition. The computer had no opinion about it.

title: DEFINITION
text: demonstrate it. Change the return to a print, run the same script, and show the TypeError two lines later when it tries to multiply None. That error is worth meeting on purpose.

title: CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING
text: quick pulse check before the break. Question C is the one to dwell on if the answers are weak.

title: 10 minutes
text: take it. The practical after the break is the long one.

title: SEGMENT 5
text: keep this short. The concept is easy; the value is in connecting it to Week 1.

title: LIVE CODING
text: make the ordering mistake live. It is the same class of failure as the unit error — no crash, wrong answer.

title: SEGMENT 6
text: this fifteen minutes saves more student time than any other in the semester.

title: TRACEBACKS
text: the format shown is Python 3.10. If Colab is on 3.11 or later there is one extra line with a ~~~^~~ marker pointing at the failing part of the expression, which is helpful rather than confusing. Say so if a student's output differs.

title: FIVE NAMES, AND ONE WITHOUT
text: produce each of the five live if you have time; at minimum produce NameError and TypeError. Seeing them made on purpose removes most of their power to frighten.

title: WORKED EXAMPLE
text: this is the first formal introduction of the AI ladder from the syllabus. 'Explain why this error is happening' is the level for Week 3; asking for whole functions is not.

title: SEGMENT 7
text: circulate and ask for the EXPECTED value before you look at anyone's code. A student who cannot state it has not understood the formula.

title: PRACTICAL — 35 MINUTES
text: commit per working function so the repository history shows the build. This is the week where git commit starts to feel useful rather than ceremonial.

title: THE POINT OF THIS WEEK
text: this figure is the thesis of the week. Do not rush it, even though the challenge is waiting.

title: CHALLENGE
text: the six planted bugs: integer division with //, operator precedence with a missing bracket, degrees where radians were needed, an if-chain whose branches are in the wrong order, a unit mismatch, and a parameter used in the wrong position in the call. Have the marking key ready naming each bug; you will need it when a team insists their diagnosis is right. Circulate with the question card and answer nothing.

title: ASSIGNMENT
text: warn them properly about the quiz format so nobody sits down to revise definitions.

text: tell them the deck continues past the end of the session.

title: MODULE SUMMARY
text: return to the objectives slide and ask for hands against each.

text: answer E is the one to read aloud. Students respect being told the reasoning behind a rule rather than just the rule.

title: END-OF-SESSION QUIZ  ·  WEEK 2
text: open the Form, project the QR, and give it exactly five minutes. Afterwards look at the responses-by-question view — any question most of the room got wrong is next week's five-minute reteach.

title: THE ONE THING TO REMEMBER
text: say the body text out loud and mean it. For a room of beginners this is the most useful thing they hear all week. Then stay behind for ten minutes — the students who need the most help will not ask in front of everyone.

title: Variables, decisions, functions — and reading errors
text: check A2 at the door — repository URL, notebook runs, README present. Anyone without a working setup goes on the office-hours list now, not in Week 5.

title: LEARNING OBJECTIVES
text: read them out, and return to this slide at the end.

title: SEGMENT 1
text: two minutes of recall, then move. Do not re-teach Week 2.

title: CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING
text: thirty seconds in pairs. If the first question is shaky, the Week 2 deck's cheat-sheet slide has it.

title: SEGMENT 2
text: take the question seriously. A calculator IS faster for one calculation, and pretending otherwise loses you the sceptics in the room — who are usually the best students.

title: TODAY STARTS WITH AN OBJECTION
text: ask the room for the answer before you give it. Someone usually says 'because you can do it lots of times', which is exactly right and better received from a student.

title: WHY BOTHER
text: labour reason three. Make the Week 10 connection explicitly; students engage far better with syntax when they can see what it is for.

title: SEGMENT 3
text: twenty-five minutes is enough. They learn this by writing it, not by hearing it.

title: VARIABLES
text: draw the box on the board and physically write a value into it, then rub it out and write another. Thirty seconds, and it lands better than any slide.

title: DEFINITION
text: demonstrate "12" + 3 live and let them read the error. It is the same TypeError they will see next week.

title: WHAT GOES WRONG
text: demonstrate 0.1 + 0.2 live. It reliably produces an audible reaction and it makes the point permanently.

title: SEGMENT 4
text: type it live, do not paste. Narrate the units as you go. The typing is where the structure is learned.

title: The parts of a function
text: ask 'what will this print?' after typing only the definition. Answer: nothing. Let that land before you add the call.

title: WORKED EXAMPLE
text: do steps 1 to 4 on the board, out loud, before opening Colab. It takes three minutes and it makes the live-coding segment much faster because the thinking is already done.

title: LIVE CODING
text: type it, run it, confirm the output matches. THEN make the deliberate mistake and let the wrong number sit on screen for a few seconds before anyone speaks. Ask: what would have told you this was wrong? Physical intuition. The computer had no opinion about it.

title: DEFINITION
text: demonstrate it. Change the return to a print, run the same script, and show the TypeError two lines later when it tries to multiply None. That error is worth meeting on purpose.

title: CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING
text: quick pulse check before the break. Question C is the one to dwell on if the answers are weak.

title: 10 minutes
text: take it. The practical after the break is the long one.

title: SEGMENT 5
text: keep this short. The concept is easy; the value is in connecting it to Week 1.

title: LIVE CODING
text: make the ordering mistake live. It is the same class of failure as the unit error — no crash, wrong answer.

title: SEGMENT 6
text: this fifteen minutes saves more student time than any other in the semester.

title: TRACEBACKS
text: the format shown is Python 3.10. If Colab is on 3.11 or later there is one extra line with a ~~~^~~ marker pointing at the failing part of the expression, which is helpful rather than confusing. Say so if a student's output differs.

title: FIVE NAMES, AND ONE WITHOUT
text: produce each of the five live if you have time; at minimum produce NameError and TypeError. Seeing them made on purpose removes most of their power to frighten.

title: WORKED EXAMPLE
text: this is the first formal introduction of the AI ladder from the syllabus. 'Explain why this error is happening' is the level for Week 3; asking for whole functions is not.

title: SEGMENT 7
text: circulate and ask for the EXPECTED value before you look at anyone's code. A student who cannot state it has not understood the formula.

title: PRACTICAL — 35 MINUTES
text: commit per working function so the repository history shows the build. This is the week where git commit starts to feel useful rather than ceremonial.

title: THE POINT OF THIS WEEK
text: this figure is the thesis of the week. Do not rush it, even though the challenge is waiting.

title: CHALLENGE
text: the six planted bugs: integer division with //, operator precedence with a missing bracket, degrees where radians were needed, an if-chain whose branches are in the wrong order, a unit mismatch, and a parameter used in the wrong position in the call. Have the marking key ready naming each bug; you will need it when a team insists their diagnosis is right. Circulate with the question card and answer nothing.

title: ASSIGNMENT
text: warn them properly about the quiz format so nobody sits down to revise definitions.

title: SEGMENT 8
text: tell them the deck continues past the end of the session.

title: MODULE SUMMARY
text: return to the objectives slide and ask for hands against each.

title: END-OF-SESSION QUIZ  ·  WEEK 3
text: open the Form, project the QR, and give it exactly five minutes. Afterwards look at the responses-by-question view — any question most of the room got wrong is next week's five-minute reteach.
